clue.text: Last of a series of twenty-four

definitions.text: Last of a series of twenty-four

parts.words: Last of a series of twenty-four
parts.note: surface reading: the final item in a set of twenty-four things, perhaps episodes or hours
setter's reading: the Greek alphabet has twenty-four letters, and the clue wants its final one

explanation.surface: Someone reaches the closing instalment of a twenty-four-part run, like a long TV series.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the clue says Greek; the number twenty-four is the only hint that the series is an alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek alphabet runs from alpha through twenty-four letters and closes with this one, hence its use for any ending.

clue.text: Casual switching of parts could get one pushed aside

indicators.note: switching of parts tells us to swap the two halves of the phrase over

parts.note: in rugby a player handed off is shoved away by an opponent's outstretched arm

explanation.surface: A careless rearrangement of roles in an organisation could see someone sidelined.
explanation.walkthrough: A hand-off is a rugby move: the ball carrier pushes a tackler away with a straight arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Done without care or thought, curt and nonchalant, which is a casual manner.

clue.text: Unequivocal dismissal upheld by court

indicators.note: in a down answer, held up means read upwards, so the word for dismissal runs bottom to top

parts.note: getting the axe means being sacked
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A worker's clear-cut sacking is confirmed by a tribunal on appeal.
explanation.walkthrough: Upheld sounds legal, confirmed on appeal, but it is the signal to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise and leaving no room for doubt, so unambiguous and strictly accurate.

clue.text: Harpo, oddly, is the source of Marxist maxim

indicators.note: oddly means in a strange way, so the name and the small word are scrambled

parts.note: the Marx brother, taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the source of a word is its beginning, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of Marxist

explanation.surface: The silent Marx brother is oddly credited with a Marxist saying.
explanation.walkthrough: Marxist suggests Karl's politics, but Harpo is one of the Marx Brothers comedy team, and only the first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A pithy saying that expresses a general truth is a short wise adage.

clue.text: Affectionate donkey, say, gets a bed of straw

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the preceding words and listen to the result rather than read their spelling

parts.note: pally means friendly or affectionate, and an ass is a donkey

explanation.surface: A fond pet donkey is rewarded with a fresh straw bed in its stable.
explanation.walkthrough: The stable scene makes the straw bed look like the donkey's reward, but the bed is the answer and the donkey is only sound.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a thin mattress stuffed with straw, an old word borrowed from French paillasse.

clue.text: Parking not allowed, making one purse one's lips

parts.note: P is the symbol for parking
an idea that is out is ruled out, not permitted

explanation.surface: A driver finds parking banned and grimaces in irritation.
explanation.definitionFit: To push the lips forward in sulky displeasure is the facial expression of a sulk.

clue.text: Living-room appropriate for the country

parts.note: surface reading: a lounge furnished in rural cottage style
setter's reading: room to live, seized by a nation that claims territory for expansion

explanation.surface: A sitting room decorated to suit a country home.
explanation.walkthrough: Appropriate is the verb to seize, not the adjective suitable; the answer is German for room to live.
explanation.definitionFit: The German term names territory a state claims as needed for its population, the Nazi justification for invading the east.

clue.text: Break in quickly, needing part of stirrup tightened

indicators.note: part of means only a section of the following words is wanted, the run of letters across them

parts.note: the letters run from the second letter of stirrup into the first of tightened

explanation.surface: A rider bursts in, needing a loose stirrup strap pulled tighter.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to enter forcibly or suddenly, a burst inward, the reverse of erupt.

clue.text: Mass of hair needs comber as result of supersonic flight

parts.note: a shock of hair is a thick untidy mass
a comber is a long curling sea wave, not a comb

explanation.surface: A tangled mop of hair needs a comb after a fast flight.
explanation.walkthrough: Comber looks like something that combs hair, but it is a breaking ocean roller.
explanation.definitionFit: An aircraft exceeding the speed of sound pushes a pressure front through the air that is heard as a sonic boom.

clue.text: Dined in college noisily

indicators.note: noisily means out loud, so the college's name is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: Eton College is the English public school

explanation.surface: Diners making a racket in a college hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is the famous English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are past participles of verbs for having a meal: one has dined, one has had a meal.

clue.text: How photographer achieves brilliance in news announcement to cry about

definitions.note: a phrase describing a means; the answer is the device that is that means

parts.note: a newsflash is a brief urgent announcement

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word for cry is read from its end back to its start

parts.note: to blub is to weep, informally

explanation.surface: A newsreader announces some event that leaves a photographer close to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the photographer's 'brilliance' is literal light, not talent.
explanation.definitionFit: Before electronic flash units, photographers lit dim scenes with single-use bulbs giving a burst of bright light.

clue.text: Way Australian bounder starts to settle for the night

indicators.note: the bounder starts, meaning it takes the front position ahead of the word for way

parts.note: a kangaroo, the Australian animal that bounds along
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A kangaroo bounding along a road begins to settle down as night falls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' looks like 'begins to', but it orders the pieces: the bounder comes first, then the way.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds perch and sleep on a branch or perch at night, which is what this verb describes.

clue.text: Main route for movement of heavy guns without damage

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the word for damage is taken out of the word for heavy guns

parts.note: artillery is the collective term for large guns
ill as a noun means harm or damage

explanation.surface: Planners pick a trunk road along which heavy guns can travel without being damaged.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond blood vessels, the word is used for any major road, river or railway carrying traffic.

clue.text: Mute, but can be understood

definitions.meaning: first meaning: not said aloud, silent
second meaning: tacitly agreed without needing to be put into words

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot talk still manages to make themselves understood.
explanation.definitionFit: An unvoiced agreement is both silent and tacitly grasped, so the adjective covers both senses.

clue.text: Have to separate female champions  confronting  each other

indicators.note: to separate two things a word must stand between them, sitting inside the pair

parts.note: two champions, each F for female plus ACE for a champion
taken as written

explanation.surface: Having to keep two women's champions apart before a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Have to reads as must, but to is the word placed between the two female aces.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes two people directly opposite one another, in each other's presence.

clue.text: Worried looks, say, at start of flight

parts.note: feeling down is feeling low or troubled

indicators.note: say tells us to take the sound of the word for looks, not its spelling

parts.note: stares are fixed looks

explanation.surface: Anxious glances from a nervous passenger as the plane takes off.
explanation.walkthrough: The flight is a flight of steps, not a plane journey: its start is at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps begins on the lower floor, so being on the lower storey puts one at its foot.

clue.text: Early boundaries in Yorkshire, say, as good as a hundred elsewhere

definitions.note: a phrase describing old divisions; the answer is one such division
definitions.meaning: first meaning: an old administrative district of Yorkshire and other northern shires

definitions.text: as good as a hundred elsewhere
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the unit equal to a hundred
definitions.meaning: second meaning: equivalent to the hundred, the county subdivision used in other parts of England

explanation.surface: A cricket boast: early fours in a Yorkshire innings count for as much as a century elsewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Boundaries and a hundred suggest cricket, but a hundred was an old subdivision of an English county; in Yorkshire and other Danish-settled shires the equivalent had a Norse name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the historical subdivision of shires in the old Danelaw, matching the hundred used in southern English counties.

clue.text: Short walk and a drink

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the final letter of walk is dropped

parts.note: to march is to walk in step

explanation.surface: A quick stroll followed by a drink at the pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Marc is a brandy distilled from the skins and pips left after grapes are pressed for wine.

clue.text: Rector of Minehead turning into a source of sympathy

indicators.note: turning means changing, so these letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the head of the Somerset town's name is its opening letter, kept alone

parts.note: the opening letter of the Somerset town

explanation.surface: A seaside vicar in Somerset becomes a consoling figure to his parish.
explanation.walkthrough: Minehead is a seaside town in Somerset; the clue splits it so that head selects the first letter of Mine.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who consoles and soothes in distress is a giver of solace, as the Holy Spirit is called.

clue.text: Testing quality of gold, like gnome

parts.note: as means in the manner of
a gnome is also a short pithy maxim, not only a garden figure

explanation.surface: Checking whether a gold garden ornament is genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: Gnome is the old word for an aphorism, from Greek, not the little bearded figure.
explanation.definitionFit: To assay a metal is to analyse it to find its purity, the standard test applied to precious ores.

clue.text: Sedate idiot

definitions.meaning: first meaning: as a verb, to drug someone into calm

explanation.surface: A calm, unhurried fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Sedate reads as the adjective calm, but it is the verb to tranquillise.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a verb for administering drugs and slang for a dim-witted person.

clue.text: Work oneself into a state to raise second XI

parts.note: to get up something is to organise or raise it, as a petition
S is the abbreviation for second
a cricket or football team is an eleven, written XI

explanation.surface: A club official gets agitated trying to field a reserve side.
explanation.walkthrough: XI is not a number to be used as letters but the usual shorthand for a sports team of eleven.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from building boiler pressure in a steam engine, so it means gathering energy or working up to action.

clue.text: It used to prevent one getting into a hole

definitions.text: It used to prevent one getting into a hole

parts.words: It used to prevent one getting into a hole
parts.note: surface reading: a device that once kept people from falling into a pit, or out of trouble
setter's reading: on a golf green, an opponent's ball lying in the line to the cup once blocked a putt, a rule since abolished

explanation.surface: Something that once kept a person out of trouble or a pit.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf situation was abolished in 1952, which is why the clue says used to.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, an opponent's ball lying between yours and the cup on the green formerly blocked the putt; now the word means any obstruction.

clue.text: Capacity gathering

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a role, as in acting in an official capacity
second meaning: a social event such as a reception

explanation.surface: A venue packed with a full crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: Capacity suggests a full house, which fits gathering, but here it means a role.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both a role someone serves in and a formal party or reception.

clue.text: Following behind dowdy old woman

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
one's behind is one's backside

explanation.surface: Someone walks along at the heels of a drab elderly lady.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes an unfashionable, plainly dressed woman, typically older and rather prim.

clue.text: E.g. Marcel's musical fare

parts.note: Hair is the 1960s rock musical
to fare is to do, as in how did you fare

explanation.surface: A Frenchman named Marcel enjoys the food or entertainment at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcel is not a diner but the inventor of the marcel wave, a crimped style.
explanation.definitionFit: A marcel is a set of deep waves put into the hair with hot tongs, so it is an example of a styled coiffure.

clue.text: Exercise power in Niger capriciously

indicators.note: capriciously means on a whim, so the country's name is rearranged arbitrarily

parts.note: the West African country, taken as written

explanation.surface: A despot wielding authority on a whim in an African state.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's rule over a kingdom is wielding sovereign authority, so the verb fits.

clue.text: End of puss, abbreviated

parts.note: surface reading: the last letter of puss, or the word shortened
setter's reading: the tail of a puss, a hare's nickname, which is short and stubby

explanation.surface: A wordplay instruction to cut the last bit off a cat's name.
explanation.walkthrough: Puss is a traditional name for a hare as well as a cat, and its stumpy tail is the end meant here.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the short erect tail of a hare, rabbit or deer, a word mainly met in hunting.

clue.text: Jolly girl starts to get rid of stilettos, perhaps

indicators.note: the girl starts, meaning her name takes the front position before the word for jolly

parts.note: Una is a girl's name
a Jolly is old slang for a Royal Marine, abbreviated RM

explanation.surface: A cheerful woman kicks off her high heels.
explanation.walkthrough: Stilettos look like shoes but are daggers here. Jolly is a noun: naval slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: To unarm is an older verb meaning to disarm, and a stiletto is a slim dagger, an example of a weapon.

clue.text: One in charge of record store

definitions.text: One in charge of record store

parts.words: One in charge of record store
parts.note: surface reading: the manager of a shop selling vinyl records
setter's reading: a store of records meaning documents, kept for history

explanation.surface: The manager of a music shop selling LPs.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a professional who keeps and catalogues historical documents in a repository of papers.

clue.text: Lead no trumps, for example

parts.note: to lead is to go before
NT is the bridge abbreviation for a no-trump contract

explanation.surface: A bridge player opens with a no-trumps lead, as an illustration.
explanation.walkthrough: Lead looks like the bridge card lead, but it is the verb go first.
explanation.definitionFit: An earlier case that serves as a model or guide for later ones is an example to follow.

clue.text: Being doomed, Nero fiddled after midnight

definitions.note: read as a noun phrase, a being who is doomed

indicators.note: fiddled means tampered with, so the emperor's name has its letters rearranged
after places the rearranged name behind the letter taken from night
the middle of the word night is wanted, its central letter alone

parts.note: the central letter of night
the Roman emperor's name, letters shuffled

explanation.surface: A nod to Nero fiddling while Rome burned, his fate sealed late at night.
explanation.walkthrough: Being is a noun, a creature, not the verb: the definition is a doomed being.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for someone or something past saving, certain to die or fail.
